title: My AI Thinks I'm Eating My Feelings (and Other Nutritional Insights) - Rami Alhamad

summary: Rami Alhamad introduces Alma, an AI nutrition companion built to make eating well simpler through personalized nutrition guidance. Alma's vision rests on three pillars: making nutrition tracking as easy as texting a friend, building powerful context around users' habits and preferences, and eventually connecting users with relevant products and restaurants. The team shipped a closed beta less than two months after incorporation, ran it for four months, and launched publicly in February. Through user feedback, they discovered people want holistic food quality insights, not just calories and macros, leading to the Alma Score—a 0-100 rating developed with Harvard adviser Dr. Eric Prim that nudges users toward healthier choices. Several engineering lessons emerged. Real-time user feedback (a dropdown toast after every interaction) proved more valuable than automated evals. Open-ended LLM tasks produced high error rates, so the team broke processing into discrete steps—food extraction, USDA database matching, caloric content—sending partial results to the client to make the experience feel faster. Users fiercely valued streaks, revealing gamification's importance. Alma continuously builds a knowledge dataset about each user, surfaced via an 'about you' orb that updates with each interaction and is editable. Proactive insights, like pairing blueberries with dark chocolate to boost vitamin C absorption, keep users engaged without requiring them to open the app. Multimodality (voice, photo, text) proved essential—users prefer different modalities depending on context. Looking forward, Alma doubles down on three areas: brand and design (as code becomes commoditized), trust and partnerships (aligning with trusted sources), and community-driven net-new data (since foundation model companies already scrape existing online data).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Alma's Vision
sections.summary: Rami introduces Alma's mission to simplify nutrition tracking. Three core pillars: easy tracking that feels like texting a friend, building powerful user context, and eventually connecting users with products and restaurants. The team builds in public and shipped quickly.

sections.title: Alma Score and User Feedback Lessons
sections.summary: Users wanted holistic food quality insights beyond calories and macros. Alma Score (0-100) was developed with Harvard's Dr. Eric Prim to nudge users toward healthier choices. Real-time user feedback via dropdown toast proved more valuable than automated evals.

sections.title: Engineering: Constraining LLMs and Step-by-Step Processing
sections.summary: Open-ended LLM tasks produce high error rates; constraining to specific tasks is essential. The team broke processing into discrete steps (food extraction, USDA matching, caloric content) and sent partial results to the client, making the experience feel faster.

sections.title: User Engagement: Streaks, Context, and Proactive Insights
sections.summary: Streaks proved unexpectedly important to users. Alma continuously builds a knowledge dataset about each user, shown via an editable 'about you' orb. Proactive insights (e.g., blueberries with dark chocolate boost vitamin C absorption) keep users engaged between sessions.

sections.title: Multimodality and Future Direction
sections.summary: Users value multimodality—voice, photo, and text—depending on context. Looking forward, Alma focuses on three areas: brand and design, trust and partnerships, and community-driven net-new data as a moat against foundation model companies.
